title: Data Visualization
subtitle: Charts, plots, histograms, scatter plots and visualization principles.
description: Turn data into meaningful visualizations and communicate patterns and relationships clearly.

blocks.text: Welcome to Lesson 8: Data Visualization. This lesson follows the course dashboard topic “Data Visualization”. The goal is to charts, plots, histograms, scatter plots and visualization principles.. Focus on understanding when this technique is useful, what assumptions it makes, and how you can check that it is working.

A visualization should answer a question, not merely decorate a report. Use bar charts to compare categories, line charts to show changes over ordered time, and scatter plots to explore relationships between numeric variables.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select R. Paste this snippet into the R editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.title: Sample 1: Data Visualization in practice
blocks.code:
scores <- c(72, 88, 91, 64)
barplot(scores, names.arg = c("A", "B", "C", "D"), ylab = "Score")

blocks.text: What to notice: focus on the part of the sample that demonstrates Charts, plots, histograms, scatter plots and visualization principles. Identify the input, the operation, and the result before making changes.

blocks.question: A chart compares the number of learners in several categories. Which chart is often appropriate?
options: A bar chart with clear labels.
A 3D pie for every value by default.
A line chart without ordered time.
A chart with no axis labels.
blocks.explanation: Bar charts are commonly useful for comparing category magnitudes.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Bar charts are commonly useful for comparing category magnitudes.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Bar charts are commonly useful for comparing category magnitudes.

blocks.text: PAGE 2 — Build the idea step by step

blocks.title: Sample 2: Data Visualization in practice
blocks.code:
practice_hours <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
plot(practice_hours, c(50, 58, 68, 74, 82), xlab = "Hours", ylab = "Score")

blocks.text: Application tip: in a real R project, choose names and structures that reveal the reason the code exists. Do not copy a snippet into a project without checking its assumptions and adapting it to the surrounding code.

blocks.question: A line chart uses calendar dates but sorts them alphabetically as text. What is the problem?
options: The font may be too large.
The x-axis order may not represent chronological time.
The data became private.
The R console changed colors.
blocks.explanation: A time series should be ordered by actual time, not alphabetic date strings.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A time series should be ordered by actual time, not alphabetic date strings.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. A time series should be ordered by actual time, not alphabetic date strings.

blocks.text: Label axes, include units, and avoid misleading scales or excessive decoration. A chart that omits units or hides uncertainty can make the same data appear to mean something different.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select R. Paste this snippet into the R editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.title: Sample 3: Data Visualization in practice
blocks.code:
wait <- c(5, 7, 6, 10, 8, 9)
hist(wait, main = "Wait times", xlab = "Minutes")

blocks.question: A plot suggests two variables move together. What conclusion is justified from that plot alone?
options: One variable definitely causes the other.
Every person has the same outcome.
There may be an association worth further investigation, not proof of causation.
No data were collected.
blocks.explanation: Visual association is not by itself evidence of a causal relationship.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Visual association is not by itself evidence of a causal relationship.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Visual association is not by itself evidence of a causal relationship.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Apply it and check your reasoning
Check outliers and missing values before interpreting patterns. A visual relationship can suggest a hypothesis, but it does not by itself prove that one variable caused another.

Before continuing, explain in your own words how this topic helps solve the dashboard goal: Turn data into meaningful visualizations and communicate patterns and relationships clearly. Try one boundary case, one normal case, and one case that should be rejected or handled differently.

blocks.question: A program repeatedly looks up a learner by a unique email address. Which structure is a natural fit?
options: A map/dictionary keyed by email, with suitable uniqueness handling.
A random number with no mapping.
A paragraph of comma-separated values that is never parsed.
A loop that guesses the correct person.
blocks.explanation: Key-value structures express lookup by identifier more directly than repeatedly scanning unrelated data.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Key-value structures express lookup by identifier more directly than repeatedly scanning unrelated data.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Key-value structures express lookup by identifier more directly than repeatedly scanning unrelated data.

blocks.question: A list contains a value at the first position. In a zero-based language, which index usually addresses it?
options: One.
The collection length.
Zero.
Minus one.
blocks.explanation: Most common programming-language arrays and lists use zero-based indexing, though language-specific structures may differ.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Most common programming-language arrays and lists use zero-based indexing, though language-specific structures may differ.
